summary: The SSH Diffie-Hellman group exchange says servers and clients should support groups of at least 1024 bits. Recent research showed this is insufficient against well-resourced attackers, so this document raises the minimum recommended modulus size to 2048 bits.

plainLanguage.summary: A lock that was once strong enough can become easy to pick with better tools. This says SSH should use a bigger, tougher lock.

questions: what is the minimum dh size for ssh
what does rfc 8270 change in rfc 4419
subtitle: SSH servers and clients should now use Diffie-Hellman groups of at least 2048 bits.

tldr.problem: RFC 4419 allowed SSH Diffie-Hellman groups as small as 1024 bits, which recent research shows is insufficient against well-resourced attackers.
tldr.mechanism: This update says SSH servers and clients SHOULD support a minimum group size of 2048 bits for the min value of the group exchange request, and clients SHOULD be able to send 3072 bits as the preferred size.
tldr.outcome: The minimum recommended modulus size for SSH Diffie-Hellman group exchange is 2048 bits.

today: RFC 8270 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4419. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why 1024 Bits Is Not Enough
sections.content:
RFC 4419 specifies a recommended minimum Diffie-Hellman (DH) modulus group size of 1024 bits for SSH. Recent research (Logjam) strongly suggests that 1024-bit DH groups can be broken by state-sponsored actors and any organization with enough computing resources. The authors showed how they break 768-bit groups and extrapolated the attack to 1024 bits.

This document therefore raises the minimum recommended size to 2048 bits, and notes that the minimum may need to increase to 3072 for forward-looking users.
sections.plainLanguage: A small padlock was fine once, but thieves now have better tools, so we need a bigger one.

sections.title: The New Size Rules
sections.content:
SSH servers and clients SHOULD support a minimum acceptable group size of 2048 bits for the min value of the SSH_MSG_KEY_DH_GEX_REQUEST message. Clients SHOULD be able to send 3072 bits as the preferred size n.

The RFC replaces two passages of RFC 4419. Servers and clients SHOULD support moduli of k bits where 2048 <= k <= 8192, with recommended minimum values for min and max of 2048 and 8192. Setting k to 3072 SHOULD be possible. In all cases, the group size SHOULD be at least 2048 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides should accept only big locks, at least 2048 sizes, and be ready to use an even bigger 3072 one.

sections.title: Interoperability
sections.content: RFC 4419 says the server should return the smallest group it knows that is larger than the size the client requested, and if it knows none, SHOULD return the largest group it knows. That stays. The following sentence is updated: in all cases the size of the returned group SHOULD be at least 2048 bits, and 3072 SHOULD be possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The server still hands over the smallest lock that is big enough, but never one smaller than 2048.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A hostile server could use backdoored DH primes to supply the g and p values, or send the calculated secret through a covert channel to a passive listener. A malicious client could cause a denial of service by making multiple connections with groups smaller than 2048 bits.

For that reason, operating systems SHOULD NOT log DH groups smaller than 2048 bits, since doing so would create an additional attack surface. No IANA actions are required.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad server might hand out a rigged lock, and a bad client might cause trouble by asking over and over, so do not write every small request in the logbook.
